title: Recognizing Transformation: Attributes of Successful Departments and Benefits of Participation in the PULSE Recognition Program
abstract: The Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences Education (PULSE) Recognition Program plays an important role in the overall work of PULSE. From our initial founding through our efforts today, PULSE Fellows involved in the Recognition Program have worked from the premise that there is value in providing summative and comparative assessment of departmental movement toward change. From our external vantage point as persons invited into departments that are engaged in self-reflection and purposeful work toward transformation, we have been able to observe ingredients found in successfully positioned departments. In an interview with PULSE Fellows who have guided departments through the Recognition Program process, we consider the question: “What are the key attributes of departments that are successfully transforming?” We will share our observations from more than a decade of work.

title: PULSE Ambassadors Campus Workshops: Developing Core Capacities and Strategies for Departmental Transformation
abstract: Despite calls for reform in undergraduate STEM education, persistent systemic barriers limit implementation of evidence-based practices. One way that the Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences Education (PULSE) addresses these challenges is through its Ambassadors Campus Workshop (ACW), a theory-driven intervention that supports development of departmental capacity for sustainable transformation. This study examined outcomes of ACW participation by analyzing survey data from 24 departments that hosted workshops between 2014 and 2023. Using thematic analysis with a Flaws of Others approach, we investigated how departments developed core capacities, implemented transformation strategies, and achieved transformation outcomes. Departments successfully developed both awareness-based capacities (e.g., understanding Vision and Change principles, valuing diversity and inclusion) and action-oriented capacities (e.g., facilitative leadership skills, collaborative decision-making). Harmonized analysis revealed two robust pathways connecting capacities to outcomes: facilitative leadership development led to structured decision-making processes and shared governance models, while Vision an

title: The Origins of PULSE as an Organizational Change Network
abstract: Most non-profit organizations emerge through the collective action of individuals who seek to work together for a common purpose or fill a perceived need. Considerable research has explored the commonalities of structure, membership, leadership, organizational behavior, and life histories of such organizations. In this article, we provide a brief look at the origin of the Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences Education (PULSE), highlighting its characteristic features in the framework of organizational theory and life histories of organizations. PULSE is distinctive among STEM higher-education organizations because (1) it was formed by education program officers who did not become members of the organization; (2) its members are academic leaders in a broad range of institutional types with diverse student audiences; (3) its organizational and communication structure was built around the principles of sociocracy; and (4) it has a rich, inclusive culture. For this project we conducted interviews with program officers at the National Science Foundation (NSF), Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), and the National Institutes of Health (NIH); workshop facilitators from Knowinnov

title: Agents of Change: Ambassadors Program Engagement as a Pathway to Professional Growth
abstract: An explicit goal of the PULSE Ambassadors program is to support STEM departments through leadership development and with resources for implementing curricular and pedagogical reform, including the recommendations of the AAAS Vision and Change report. The heart of the program is a robust network of faculty leaders from a diverse array of institutions across the country who serve as Ambassadors. This network grew from commitments to parity among Carnegie classifications and strong representation of colleges and universities that serve PEERs (persons excluded because of their ethnicity or race; i.e., HBCU, MSI, and HSI institutions). In this research, we investigate how Ambassadors have transferred elements of their work in the network to other areas of their professional lives, including their own departments, leadership roles, professional organizations, and beyond. Through 12 semi-structured interviews, Ambassadors share their own stories of change. Four primary themes emerged from these stories: Resistance to change, Being an outsider, Skill development, and Connections.

title: PULSE: A Distinct and Necessary Leader in Undergraduate STEM Education Reform
abstract: The Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences (PULSE) arose from a series of meetings hosted by HHMI, NSF, and NIH. Forty current and former department chairs, across all institution types of higher education, were asked to identify practical strategies for transforming undergraduate life sciences education. Distinct from other STEM reform efforts, PULSE focused on the academic department as the key unit of sustainable change, targeting entire teaching-and-learning systems rather than isolated practices. Central to PULSE’s approach is a coordinated strategy built on three programs: the Ambassadors Program, the Recognition Program, and Regional Networks. Together, these programs foster cultural and organizational change at the departmental level. Colleges and universities can use any or all of these programs to address their distinctive path towards departmental change. What began as a time-limited initiative evolved into a self-sustaining organizational change network – PULSE. Its growth was the result of intentional organizational design, built on the principles of sociocracy (https://www.sociocracyforall.org/), notably for providing a structure and set of practices to promote i

title: Expanding the Impact: Leveraging PULSE to Transform STEM Education Through Workforce Development for Economic Mobility
abstract: PULSE products and services have successfully supported undergraduate life science departments in their efforts to enhance student-centered pedagogies. They are also adaptable for departments in other STEM disciplines and the broader STEM community. This article describes an example of how PULSE can help departments respond to the need to incorporate workforce development skills into STEM education programs, to address economic mobility for students. This case study highlights the ability of PULSE to collaborate and synergize with existing and developing STEM initiatives, using recent examples in Puerto Rico and Philadelphia.

title: Leading Departments, Empowering Change: An Introduction to the Special Issue
abstract: The introduction to the Transformative Dialogues special issue outlines the context in which the Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences Education (PULSE) organization emerged and evolved. This essay briefly summarizes each contribution in this special issue featuring PULSE’s programs and impact on department-level organizational change.

title: The Power of Kinship: PULSE Came Together to Solve a Problem, and Along the Way, Created a Family
abstract: The Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences Education (PULSE) functions as a kinship-centered community of practice (CoP) where reciprocal obligation, shared problem-solving, and mutual aid convert collegial ties into rewarding resources (mentoring, voice, feedback, tools). PULSE’s Dynamic Governance cultivates kinship-based reciprocity, converting community ties into rewarding personal experiences in the traditionally siloed academy. In Social Exchange terms, reciprocity norms sustain ongoing contribution. In Job Demands-Resources terms, these resources drive engagement and buffer burnout. The result is faculty who remain continuously engaged educators even in demanding departmental climates. Here, we share the experiences of onboarding new PULSE Fellows and how the PULSE community’s structure and kinship supported efficient integration and rewarding contributions to the organization. These resources enhance engagement, buffer burnout, and reduce turnover intentions, reframing integration as co-evolution between faculty and institutions rather than competition today. The PULSE kinship-centered CoP can serve as a model for other organizations and collaborations in higher educat

title: Among Equals: Sociocracy as a Means of Improving Academic Collaboration and Participation
abstract: Every self-governing organization needs a structure that ensures it can make the decisions necessary for its operation and preservation. These structures can range from a centralized authority entrusted with all decisions to a consensus-based model whereby all interested parties must agree before a decision is reached. This article describes why PULSE chose sociocracy, an inclusive form of governance based on consent of the governed. We describe the key features of sociocracy and explain how it has been valuable not only for ensuring a collegial atmosphere and effective decision-making among PULSE Fellows, but how it has affected the ways in which PULSE Fellows operate in their own spheres of influence. We propose that this form of governance can be used in a variety of settings to foster community, collaboration, and shared decision-making.

title: From Vision to Action: Using Pathway Models to Identify Key Steps in Catalyzing Department-Level Transformation
abstract: The Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences Education (PULSE) seeks to improve undergraduate STEM education for students from all backgrounds and regions across the United States, in all higher education settings. To achieve this, PULSE engages academic departments in three complementary programs (Recognition, Ambassador, and Regional Networks) that provide department-level professional development aimed at developing skills and knowledge relevant to promoting change in their educational programs aligned with recommendations of Vision and Change in Undergraduate Biology Education (Brewer & Smith, 2011). These programs emphasize how institutional change works and build practical skills for engaging colleagues, holding productive discussions, and reaching consensus. To support evaluation efforts for continuous improvement, PULSE made the causal links between program activities and outcomes explicit by creating program-specific pathway models grounded in a unifying Theory of Change (ToC). Pathway modeling, a widely used tool for evaluation planning, clarified how program activities develop core capacities, enable transformation strategies, and culminate in department-level outcome

title: PULSE Regional Networks: Different Approaches to Drive Departmental Change Across Diverse Educational Landscapes
abstract: To facilitate its goal of fostering department transformation, the Partnership for Undergraduate Life Sciences Education (PULSE) organizes some of its work into five geographic regions and leverages the expertise of the PULSE Fellows in each region. This article examines how these Regional Networks have driven department-level changes through outreach activities, use of the PULSE Rubrics as a diagnostic tool to help departments to advance the Vision and Change recommendations, and implementation of the PULSE framework to address local needs and challenges. We present impact data through Regional Network activities and identify commonalities in successes and challenges across all the geographic regions. Through reports from the Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, Northwest, and Midwest Great Plains, we highlight each Regional Network’s accomplishments in influencing the adoption of PULSE strategies to implement the Vision and Change recommendations to transform departments.

title: How are the Dynamic and Interactive Elements of Resilience Reflected in Higher Education Literature? A Critical Narrative Review.
abstract: There has been a proliferation of papers on resilience in universities in recent years, many of them focused on how educators can make students more resilient. Yet the meaning of the term is nebulous, and critics argue that the focus on individuals obscures wider systemic dysfunction. This paper reports on a critical narrative review informed by a multidimensional framework called the Dynamic and Interactive Model of Resilience (DIMoR) (ahmed Shafi, Templeton et al., 2020; ahmed Shafi, Middleton et al., 2023). We found three critical themes in the extant literature: a troubling lack of complexity and coherence in how resilience is conceptualised; unsupportable assumptions inherent in typical resilience-training interventions; and incompatibility between traditional scientific investigative methods and the dynamic and interactive dimensions of resilience. We argue for a more considered approach to resilience within the sector, looking to co-create with all community members the conditions that are supportive of resilience: namely, connection, communication, compassion, care, and challenge. By profiling five illustrative examples from the literature, we suggest a way forward for prac

title: Is There Room for Spirituality in Science?
abstract: This paper explores the dissonant worldview of western-trained scientists who are taught to ‘think and write scientifically’: that is, to ask rational, fact-based questions and remove all personal reflection or emotion, and Indigenous scientists who hold a holistic and relation-based view. Using examples and experiences gained from leading a third-year university land-based learning science course, we explore the possibility of incorporating spirits and spirituality into science and imagine a new definition of thinking and writing scientifically – one that includes both heart and spirit along with mind and body – and comes from a place of humility and that reflects a willingness to engage with the immeasurable.

title: The First-Year University Experience: A Qualitative Analysis of Biological and Biomedical Students’ Reflections on the Challenges of Transition
abstract: Reflective and self-reflection practices are important skills that allow students to consider how well they have done and how they will improve their performance in the future. They are, therefore, essential attributes that support student learning, performance, and success in their future career. Our analysis of multinational, first-year biological and biomedical science students’ reflective narratives and reports showed that these students usually face remarkable challenges during the transition to university life. The authors suggest solutions and strategies to help students who face these challenges to improve their learning and success.

title: Chairing the Conversation: Learning Leadership Through Netflix’s "The Chair"
abstract: This iterative Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) project explores how online graduate students experience a television show (Netflix’s The Chair) as a threaded case study in an asynchronous, eight-week organizational leadership course. Although implemented within a typically asynchronous program, the instructor assigned small groups to meet synchronously to discuss applying course content to the television series. Additionally, students wrote an organizational analysis paper on the fictitious Pembroke University and submitted two reflection assignments. Action research methodology (McNiff, 2013; Mertler, 2020) informed this SoTL project using quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis tools. In total, 16 students over three course iterations participated; 11 completed the six-question survey, and student reflections generated 60 pages of text. The findings demonstrated that survey respondents met the intended course learning outcomes and positively rated the synchronous peer interaction. The qualitative text analysis of students’ reflections about The Chair and the synchronous discussion yielded four primary themes: (a) theory came to life, (b) connections

title: Serious Games, Student Motivation, and Emergent Learning: Autoethnographic Insights From an Environmental Studies Classroom
abstract: ‘Serious’ games are growing in popularity as a teaching tool, but what are they teaching? In theory, games let us experience real-world issues and complications in a ‘safe’ space for learning, one where we can experiment with approaches and learn from mistakes. But an ontological tension is that the ‘unreality’ of games can encourage people to modify their behaviours in unexpected ways, impacting the kinds of learning that can take place. This essay uses an autoethnographic approach, drawing on structured vignette analysis to reflect on personal classroom experiences of teaching with games (Fishbanks and Climate Hazard Resilience Forums) in the field of environmental studies. Classroom experiences are contextualised using gamer motivation profiles as a theoretical lens, illustrating the ways in which different students interpret and enact ‘games’, which may yield unexpected outcomes and learnings. Games can offer a rich opportunity for students to experience negotiation and collaboration, and experiment with alternative environmental imaginaries. But along the way, as students interpret and enact the ‘roles and rules’ of games in different ways, potentially aligning with different

title: Journeying into SoTL: A Transformative Experience Through the SPARK-ENG Professional Learning
abstract: In engineering education, the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) offers a pathway for educators to advance their professional learning and teaching practices. However, the perception of SoTL as less rigorous than traditional disciplinary research often discourages faculty engagement. Additionally, while engineering educators possess strong technical expertise in their respective fields, they often lack the knowledge, skills, and resources necessary for conducting educational research. These challenges were particularly evident among engineering educators at our university, a major Canadian institution. To address these gaps, we developed the SPARK-ENG program—a modular professional learning initiative providing support for engineering educators in their SoTL journey.

title: Student as Teacher: How Video Assessment Impacts Motivation & Performance in Online Chemistry Courses
abstract: As instructors seek more effective ways to support student learning in STEM disciplines, traditional exams continue to raise concerns around engagement and depth of understanding, particularly in online course formats. In chemistry education, where conceptual reasoning and problem-solving are essential, there is a growing interest in alternative formats of assessment that encourage confidence and long-term retention. This small-scale study explores the impact of a video-based assessment intervention implemented in an online general chemistry course at a large, public research university. By replacing selected exam questions with student-created teach-back videos, the intervention aimed to assess content mastery and shifts in student motivation and confidence. Using a survey-based design, the study (n=36) compares performance between students who completed the video-assessment and those who did not, offering insight into how assessment alterations may enhance student learning and self-efficacy in STEM education.

title: “Inspired by Our Desire to Learn": Answerability in a Mini-Museum University Assignment
abstract: This article examines “answerability” (Patel, 2016) as an alternative to dominant paradigms of accountability in higher education assessment through a Scholarship of Teaching and Learning study in a U.S. undergraduate course on learning outside of formal classrooms. I focus on one arts-based assignment—a “mini-museum”—in which students curated collections representing learning. Applying Patel’s coordinates of research answerability to students’ mini-museums showcased how their work explored learning as transformation, knowledge as partial and contextual, and contexts as shaped by intersecting systems of oppression. Re-reading the narratives of two students further illustrates how alternative assessments can honor diverse contexts and identities. Rather than being accountable to predetermined learning outcomes or knowledge demonstrated through traditional tests or papers, creative, multimodal assignments, such as the mini-museum, encourage students to interrogate and dialogue about their own experiences, to take risks, to co-create new knowledge, and to advocate for learning spaces of refuge and transformation. Examining these assignments through the lens of answerability suggests t

title: A Survey of Student Opinions About a Haiku Writing Assignment
abstract: This study examined the instructional value of a haiku writing assignment (HWA) from the graduate students’ perspective via a survey of their opinions. Fifty-eight students wrote and submitted haiku over the course of a semester. A 10-item survey instrument was used to elicit students’ opinions about the assignment. The probability of responses to each of the items on the survey was compared to chance occurrence. Chi-Square tests found that students enjoyed the assignment and the example haiku; they believed that the assignment helped them grasp concepts and be more engaged with the course content; and recommended the use of such an assignment. However, students did not believe that this assignment aided their learning or influenced their course grade. They also reported no intentions of writing haiku for academic or other purposes on their own. It is concluded that though there is value in a haiku writing assignment, it must be used selectively. The data and implications for using such assignments are discussed. .

title: Buffalo Rock Tipi Camp: A Collection of Poems Exploring Etuaptmumk and the Common Ground Between Western and Indigenous Science
abstract: This collection of poems was written by a third-year Biology student as part of her final project in Common Ground: Learning from the Land, an experiential field course held entirely outdoors. The course asks students to consider the natural world from both a western and Indigenous scientific perspective and to consider the lessons that come from plants and trees, from insects and animals, and from water, wind, and fire. It asks students to explore the principle of Etuaptmumk, or Two-Eyed seeing, a way of seeing the world around us that honors the strength of both Indigenous and western ways of knowing. These poems and the heartfelt authors’ notes reflect a three-way dialogue between the students, their instructor, and Napii eek stunn, the Oldman’s River valley, where the students camped in tipis and were guided by Blackfoot Elders. The Common Ground course encourages students to broaden their perspective and challenge their beliefs about what science is and is not, and the role of spirituality and interconnectedness in science. It teaches them how to listen and learn from the land.

title: Celebrating Advancements in Decoding the Disciplines
abstract: This issue of Transformative Dialogues: Teaching and Learning Journal focuses on Decoding the Disciplines, a theory that helps us understand student learning difficulties and make appropriate pedagogical choices. Articles in this issue are focused on identifying and addressing bottlenecks, new and alternative approaches to the traditional Decoding interview, innovations in Decoding, and connecting Decoding with broader theories and communities.

title: Decoding and Disrupting AI in Higher Education: Rethinking the Challenges for Pedagogy, Learning, and Academic Integrity
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education is transforming how teaching, learning, and assessment are designed and experienced. Tools like generative AI models now perform tasks traditionally associated with student learning—such as writing essays or solving complex problems—raising urgent questions about academic integrity, student engagement, and pedagogical practice. This paper applies the Decoding and Disrupting the Disciplines (DDD) framework to examine how AI is disrupting foundational aspects of learning, particularly in the stages where instructors identify cognitive barriers, model expert thinking, and assess understanding. Focusing specifically on the first five steps of the framework, the study argues that these areas are where AI is currently exerting the greatest and most immediate impact. While the later stages of Decoding involve institutional change and knowledge dissemination, this paper concentrates on classroom-level interventions where educators are already adapting their approaches in response to AI's presence. Drawing on recent literature, the analysis highlights how uncritical use of AI may reduce productive cognitive struggle

title: Decoding Spatial Empathy: Using Digital Storytelling to Overcome Barriers in Geographic Understanding
abstract: This study applies the Decoding the Disciplines framework to address a persistent bottleneck in geographic education: students' difficulty developing spatial empathy in increasingly hybridized learning environments. Spatial empathy—the ability to deeply connect with and understand places and their inhabitants beyond cognitive recognition—requires students to overcome ontological and epistemological barriers rooted in colonial perspectives of space. Through careful analysis, we identify expert mental moves that geographers employ, including multi-sensory engagement with place, recognition of temporal layers and multiple narratives, embodied spatial cognition, connecting personal experience to broader contexts, and transferring spatial understanding across physical and digital realms. We created immersive 3D audio experiences featuring pandemic-related campus narratives and measured their impact on 47 university students. Results demonstrate significant differences in emotional responses between students who experienced campus closure (more negative emotional tone, higher intensity) versus those who didn't, though both groups reported high empathy levels. title: Mentoring via a Decoding Interview: Helping an Instructor Navigate a Bottleneck in Organic Chemistry
abstract: A useful way to encourage faculty to develop pedagogical content knowledge is to identify bottlenecks that students face. A one-on-one interview of an instructor by a disciplinary novice can identify the challenges that a novice learner faces. Teaching electron motion in organic chemistry is an example of a bottleneck that poses significant challenges for both students to learn and instructors to teach. Students have usually never encountered the ideas associated with moving electrons in a chemical reaction to help predict products; instructors struggle to help learners understand the generalizable facets of chemical reactivity. A sixty-minute Decoding interview was conducted between an instructor with expertise in chemistry with little background in Decoding (IAS) and an experienced interviewer with little background in chemistry (JM). The interview was conducted to better delineate the bottleneck of electron motion for the instructor. The interview highlights the information that can be gleaned through dialogue, as well as demonstrating the value of mentoring, the importance of reflection, and the way that emotions can affect learning.

title: Toward a Future for SoTL in Art History via Decoding the Disciplines
abstract: This is the first in a series of planned publications demonstrating intersections between Decoding the Disciplines and the still-emerging Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) in Art History. To this end and as potential inspiration for others, this article presents personal and professional narratives along with “self-decoded” art history lessons. The narratives chart this emerging SoTL scholar’s attempt to reconcile conflicting identities on personal and professional, as well as procedural scales by mapping their individual lived experience as a first-generation, working-class student onto the broader “journey” narrative commonly applied to the transition from disciplinary research to interdisciplinary SoTL work, and extrapolating this to potential applications of the Decoding the Disciplines framework to the field of Art History. It also proposes a proof of concept aimed at establishing the Decoding the Disciplines paradigm as a central operating framework for future SoTL work in Art History by offering sample lessons on two essential competencies of the field, aesthetic description and visual analysis, as a call for Decoding’s use as a common language to coalesce ongoing,

title: Embedding Decoding Theory in the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL): A Translational Theory to Practice, Practice to Theory Bridge
abstract: In this critical essay, the authors delineate bottlenecks related to the Decoding the Disciplines movement’s long-term goal of more fully integrating itself within the scholarship of teaching and learning (SoTL), especially in navigating the complex and multi-disciplinary relationship(s) between theory, practice, and scholarship. The authors posit a distinctive role for the Decoding framework as a conceptual bridge that enables practitioners to integrate theories of their own choosing into their SoTL work, thereby enriching both research and teaching practice.

title: Reimagining Decoding the Disciplines: Revealing Hidden Expertise in Institutional Practices
abstract: This article explores the adaptation of the Decoding the Disciplines (DtD) framework from its traditional classroom context to the broader institutional arena, specifically targeting student affairs. Originally designed to make disciplinary expert thinking explicit, DtD has been reimagined here to uncover and address hidden institutional bottlenecks that impede student success. Using South Mountain Community College (SMCC) as a case study to explore this adaptation of the DtD framework, we document the transformation of the framework into a tool for diagnosing and decoding complex administrative processes—such as admissions, enrollment, and financial aid—that often present significant challenges for students. At SMCC, the authors engaged in a series of workshops where student affairs staff, redefined as “insiders,” engaged in systematic reflection and cross-departmental collaboration to identify both procedural and emotional barriers. The findings underscore the potential of this adapted framework to reveal tacit institutional knowledge, challenge entrenched assumptions, and promote structural change. This work not only extends the applicability of the DtD model but also offers act

title: No Student Should Be an Island: A Peer-Approach to Decoding and Disrupting
abstract: This article describes a new student-based approach to Decoding and Disrupting. This approach consists of an educational programme that works with a multidisciplinary group of undergraduate students, so-called Culture Fellows. In the programme, the students learn about theories on disciplinary cultures and their practices, Decoding the Disciplines, and communication. The programme focuses on the implicitness of disciplinary practices and how to explore them, i.e., it seeks to address the importance of making disciplinary practices, norms, and values more accessible to students. Within the programme, the Culture Fellows use a student-based variant of the Decoding the Disciplines Paradigm that we call ‘Culture Quest’. The Culture Quest supplies students with the tools to question, explore, and decode their respective disciplines and practices. Disciplinary practices often remain implicit because lecturers, with their wealth of experience and expertise in their discipline, may be operationally blind and thus no longer aware of the fact that certain practices might need to be explained. This lack of explanation or explicitness can lead to students feeling bewildered, confused or puzzle

title: Flash Decoding with Analogies, Game Mechanics, and AI Assistance: Alternatives to the Traditional Decoding Interview
abstract: For over 30 years, the Decoding theory has helped educators break through student learning bottlenecks. Now, new methods and tools for Decoding and Disrupting have arrived. This article shares theory and practice on “Flash Decoding” with analogies and game mechanics as two of the most efficient and engaging ways to uncover the mental move as alternatives to the Decoding interview. With access to generative artificial intelligence, Flash Decoding using game mechanics can be achieved by even the busiest of professors. The first half of the article explains analogy-based Decoding, and the second half explains game mechanics-based Decoding.

title: Analysing what-if-questions as a move in Decoding Interviews
abstract: Decoding the Disciplines often involves helping instructors uncover hidden expertise. Suitable questions can facilitate this process. Here, we analyze and discuss the question “What would happen if you don’t do what experts do?” using parts of a recorded Decoding interview. This question can help to delve deep into expertise. Based on the recorded interview we conclude that several features contribute to this: The question helps to provoke lateral thinking and to move from vague to concrete descriptions of expertise.

title: Writing as a Critical, Cultural, and Emotional Terrain
abstract: This article examines the cognitive and emotional bottlenecks that students encounter in intensive writing courses, highlighting how these challenges emerge across diverse student populations. Drawing on classroom practice, student narratives, and writing studies scholarship, I argue that writing difficulties should be reframed not as failures but as moments of intellectual and emotional friction where learning is most possible. Two major bottlenecks, confusing information delivery with argumentation and internalized emotional blocks such as self-doubt, linguistic insecurity, and academic trauma, are explored in depth. These are further broken into sub-bottlenecks of observation, imagination, skill development, and revision, each scaffolded to help students move from passive summarizers to confident arguers. Strategies such as emotional decoding, multimodal composition, and reflective revision are presented as tools to cultivate voice, agency, and rhetorical flexibility. By integrating theoretical framing with practical classroom interventions, this model resists deficit framings and affirms diverse literacies. Ultimately, bottlenecks, once decoded, become gateways, not only to str

title: Bottlenecks in the Logic Classroom
abstract: A “bottleneck” is a point in a course where many students get stuck, and have problems to progress further. I identify seven bottlenecks in the introductory symbolic logic classroom. Using the “Decoding the Disciplines” framework, I then propose lesson plans designed to overcome these bottlenecks.

title: Dialogue, Process, and Reflection: Notes on Creating a Decoding Organization
abstract: In this article we introduce ourselves and invite those new to the burgeoning Decoding organization, and/or to Decoding itself, to join this community of Decoders/Disrupters. We each describe our recent experiences as co-chairs of the Decoding organization in order to highlight key features of the Decoding/Disrupting model and frameworks of interest to newcomers. Specifically, we focus on the following features of Decoding/Disrupting: perspective-taking, the value of “outsider” frames of reference, and a focus on process and relationship-building. We reflect on what we have learned from our experiences as co-chairs about Decoding/Disrupting and creating an organization. We describe next steps for developing a Decoding organization that will serve as a home base for Decoders and Disruptors in a variety of geographic locations and epistemological contexts.

title: The Application of Practice as Research Methodologies to Interdisciplinary Teaching and Learning
abstract: The piece that follows is a reflection that engages existing research in the areas of Practice as Research (PaR) and Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL), with research and pedagogy in embodied cognition. It reflects the complexities of engaging in a process-driven model for an assignment that values the generative nature of failure. As an artist/researcher in the field of dance, I bring embodied knowing into spaces where the mind/body divide is still upheld and valued. Within PaR models, process has value beyond the output of the artifact, and failure is the doorway to potentiality as it is functionalized in a creative/dance process. It is a traceable attempt on my part to deliberately bring the messiness, community, rhizomic thinking, discovery, engagement, affect, “aha!” moments, and multiplicity into the classroom in the same way they accompany me in the dance studio and choreographic process. I believe it takes a deliberate act to take a reflective perspective to teaching and learning (SoTL) and creative research. This is my deliberate weave

title: Plagiarism Due to Cultural Misunderstanding of ESL Students: Higher Education Faculty Members’ Perspectives
abstract: Plagiarism continues to be an issue in online and traditional higher education. Previous research discusses the three ways that higher education defines plagiarism being theft, deception, and misunderstanding. While institutions and instructors approach the issue of plagiarism much differently, it has left room for different interpretations of some of the aspects of the plagiarism of misunderstanding. There are three categories of misunderstanding in plagiarism, including cultural, generational, and academic enculturation. This article focuses on the aspect of cultural misunderstanding. The sample consisted of (n = 333) online faculty members. The results displayed significant differences in how faculty members approach plagiarism due to misunderstanding with regards to intentional plagiarism and coaching for English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) or multicultural students.

title: Settler Starting Points: Mapping a Model for Decolonising Practices in Higher Education
abstract: Arising from a literature review and an autoethnographic, autobiographical narrative study, this theoretical-conceptual paper presents Settler Starting Points (SSP), developed for use by non-Indigenous, settler educators, in post-secondary education in Canada (and potentially beyond), who seek to decolonise and centre Indigenous Ways of Knowing, Being, Doing, and Relating in their teaching and curricular practices. Identifying key challenges and opportunities, the author maps possible trailheads to begin a journey of decolonising one’s own epistemology and ontology. Through a visual representation and textual description of the process model and a series of questions for critical self-reflection, SSP incorporates a holistic Indigenous framework - intellectual, spiritual, emotional, and physical dimensions - to present four starting point: humility (epistemic modesty), relationality (co-curriculum making), responsibility (authentic ally), and land (place-based attention).

title: Transparency and Alignment: Challenges and Benefits in Switching to Standards-Based Grading
abstract: This collective self-study explores our switch from traditional grading practices to implementing standards-based grading in a large, lecture- and discussion-based course. Reflective findings from the instructional team, consisting of a lead faculty instructor and graduate student teaching assistants, include logistical challenges involved with making this change, namely questions around communicating grading progress to students and ensuring accurate capturing of student progress as aligning to standards-based grading rubrics. We also noted an increased perception of student autonomy and engagement with the course material. Recommendations for future study on this topic include the need for continued inclusion of graduate student teaching assistant perspectives when redeveloping course assessment structures.

title: Spoiled for Choice: A Multi-Year Study of Student Topic Selection in Psychology Courses
abstract: The provision of student choice has become an increasingly popular instructional strategy in post-pandemic higher education, but the evidence to support the practice is mixed and its effectiveness appears to be dependent on what the instructor wishes the students to gain through the experience. The present study examines student artifacts—case studies selected by students across eight undergraduate psychology courses over the courses of a five-year period (n=133)—with the goal of identifying potential theoretical explanations for those choices that point to ways in which the assignment (and others like it) might be constructively modified in the future.

title: Dispositional Outcomes of Community-Based Learning in a Graduate-Level Consultation Course
abstract: Community-based learning (CBL) is an effective pedagogy to provide meaningful, professionally oriented, graduate-level training while also serving the needs of community partners. The current study examined the experiences of students in a master’s level school psychology program as they engaged in a CBL project focused on the curation of intervention resources for local school districts. The authors employed a thematic narrative analysis of reflection papers, and overarching themes of optimism, awareness, fulfillment, and commitment were identified. The findings suggest that although the CBL strategy used in this experience was mainly transactional, it proved to be transformative for the students, as it led to a change in their dispositions. .
